cards.html: The recommendation shipped. Most people stop here and never learn whether they were right. Closing the loop is the discipline of going back after the decision to check the outcome. It turns a one-time analysis into a track record, and, bluntly, it is how you build a promotion case: "I found a six-figure opportunity and the fix recovered most of it in year one" is a sentence you can only say if you went back and measured.

At decision timeAt follow-up
Document the decision that was madeMeasure the actual impact
Define the success metric and its targetCompare it to what you predicted
Set a follow-up dateWrite down what you learned
Assign an ownerShare the result with the same stakeholders

The half everyone skips is the first. If you do not write down the target and the follow-up date at decision time, the follow-up never happens; there is always something more urgent. So book it the day the decision is made: "Android payment rebuild approved. Target: 6.0% to 8.0% conversion within 30 days of launch. I'll check on the 30th. I own it."

The single most valuable step is comparing actual to predicted, because that is where your judgment improves. Parla's Android payment redesign launched on November 20. Measured carelessly, it would have fooled you badly:

WhenAndroid conversionWhat was happening
Before launch6.0%The old payment screen
Redesign live6.5%New design, normal traffic
Nov 25 to Dec 19.5%New design plus the Black Friday sale
After the sale6.5%New design, normal traffic again

"Close the loop" during Black Friday week and you would report a 3.5-point lift and credit the redesign for all of it. You would be wrong. The redesign was worth about half a point (6.0% to 6.5%, small but real). The big jump was the promotion, and it vanished when the sale ended. Closing the loop honestly means waiting for a clean window and separating what your change did from what else was going on. Sanity-checking a result and closing the loop are the same reflex applied at two different moments.

cards.s: The loop feeds the next question
cards.html: The last checkbox, share the result, is not a courtesy. When Sam tells Nadia "we predicted a 2-point lift and got 0.5 from the design alone; the rest was the sale", the next analysis has started. The real question is now sharper: is a half-point structural lift worth the rebuild, and what would move the needle more? Every closed loop hands you a better question than the one you started with, and sends you back to the top of this track with a fuzzy ask that is already half sharp.

Fill this out before you present anything important:

  • The finding (with a number): what did you actually find?
  • Sanity check passed? Volume, range, sum, trend, source and the smell test; mix shift and correlation traps ruled out?
  • What it means: the finding in money, users or risk.
  • The ask: the action, its cost, and its expected value (as a range, honestly).
  • The audience version: exec, product, engineering or data?
  • Success metric and target: the number that will tell you it worked, and by when.
  • Follow-up date and owner.

1. Which half of the checklist is usually skipped?
  2. Why not measure during Black Friday week?
🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

1: The decision-time half: target, date and owner. 2: The sale is a confound that moves the metric by itself; you'd credit the redesign with the promotion's effect.

quiz.q: Which half of the close-the-loop checklist is usually skipped?
quiz.why: Write the target, date and owner the day the decision is made.

quiz.why: The promotion moves the metric by itself.

Which step improves your judgment most?
